plot_extraction.response_text:
At a packed public lecture, a pedagogue condemns conventional school discipline before defending corporal punishment as a Russian tradition. He unveils his invention: an automated, supposedly impartial flogging machine designed for schools, prisons, the military, workplaces, and even families. He explains that weighted coupons or coins determine the number of strokes, while the machine restrains offenders and cannot be stopped without special keys.

During a demonstration with a leather dummy, the inventor predicts that the machine will eradicate crime, idleness, and financial problems. As he displays a heavy commemorative chronometer, it slips from his hand into the machine’s receptacle. The apparatus activates, traps him, and begins flogging him relentlessly. The keys cannot be found, and attempts to stop or damage the machine fail as the stroke counter climbs into the thousands.

Eventually, the fire brigade destroys the machine after 1,650 strokes, ending both the apparatus and enthusiasm for the idea. The inventor survives but becomes permanently calmer, gentler, and melancholy. He returns to teaching, becomes beloved by his pupils, and never revisits his invention.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is a comic satirical tale built around an absurd technological invention and a rigorously prepared reversal. Its manner combines social realism, mock-scientific exposition, bureaucratic parody, and farce. The setting is initially rendered with composed, observational precision: the crowded provincial hall, the bright dresses and uniforms, the attentive silence, and even the buzzing fly create a credible public occasion before the grotesque machine comes into focus. This sober framing makes the increasingly outrageous premise seem temporarily plausible.

The narration is third-person, omniscient, and outwardly restrained. The narrator generally reports events with the calm authority of a public chronicler, allowing the characters’ words and actions to expose their own folly. Irony is pervasive but rarely explained. Elevated phrases such as “mechanical justice,” “most respected audience,” and “beloved fatherland” are placed beside brutality, vanity, and incompetence, producing a strong gap between official language and moral reality. The narrator occasionally intervenes with ceremonious formulations—“It is difficult to describe” or “it should be said”—which imitate sober historical reporting while sharpening the comedy.

Much of the story consists of the lecturer’s extended monologue. His speech is verbose, repetitive, self-important, and carefully graduated from pedagogical argument to nationalist enthusiasm and utopian prophecy. He relies on rhetorical questions, enumerations, scriptural and literary allusions, patriotic commonplaces, technical terminology, and constant direct address to “ladies and gentlemen.” His argument parodies intellectual rationalisation: cruelty is not rejected but modernised, depersonalised, quantified, and presented as humane progress. The formal eloquence and apparent logic conceal a grotesque premise, so the speech becomes a sustained exercise in dramatic irony.

The diction alternates between ornate public rhetoric and exact mechanical description. Words associated with education, administration, engineering, punishment, and measurement dominate: “celerity,” “indicator,” “scale of severity,” “statistical and revisionary purposes,” “equipoise,” and numbered degrees and strokes. Lists of institutions, components, punishments, and social benefits create a bureaucratic texture. Quantities, weights, coins, keys, springs, rods, and counters give the fantasy material specificity. This excessive precision is itself comic, suggesting a mentality that can calculate suffering without comprehending it. Period details and Russian institutional terms contribute to the historical and provincial atmosphere, while occasional explanatory footnotes reinforce the pseudo-documentary effect.

Sentence structure shifts according to function. Descriptive passages use balanced, moderately long sentences with accumulating clauses. The lecture favours long periodic constructions, parallelism, catalogues, qualifications, and emphatic conclusions. During the catastrophe, the prose becomes shorter and more fragmented. Exclamations, cries, commands, ellipses, onomatopoeic sounds, and isolated counter readings accelerate the action: “3180, 3181, 3182….” The repeated numbers act as a mechanical refrain, registering time, pain, and the machine’s indifference. This contrast between discursive slowness and frantic action is central to the story’s pacing.

Dialogue is sharply individualised through comic motifs. The deaf governor repeatedly proposes excessive punishment, while his pug-dog supplies a barking echo. The attendant combines devotion with ludicrous practical concern about the lecturer’s new trousers. The inventor’s polished abstractions collapse into cries, insults, and pleas once he becomes the victim. This change in register exposes the difference between discussing violence and experiencing it. Minor characters are sketched economically through a single behaviour, accessory, or verbal habit, giving the tale the crowded quality of a staged comic scene.

Structurally, the story proceeds as a demonstration with an inevitable trap. The concealed apparatus creates initial curiosity; the long explanation delays its operation while planting every mechanism required for the climax. The lecturer repeatedly stresses that the machine cannot be stopped, that any round object can activate it, and that heavier objects produce more strokes. His display of the heavy chronometer therefore triggers a reversal that is surprising in timing but fully prepared in retrospect. The inventor is literally subjected to the impersonal system he praises, making the ending a form of poetic justice and a physical enactment of the phrase “hoist with his own petard.”

The humour escalates from dry irony to grotesque slapstick. The lecturer’s accidental capture, the fruitless search for keys, the concern over his trousers, the shattered sword, the injured dignitary, and the eventual arrival of the fire brigade form a sequence of increasingly chaotic attempts at rescue. Beneath the comedy lies genuine cruelty: the victim’s suffering is prolonged, public, numerically recorded, and met by institutional helplessness. The machine is frightening precisely because it performs violence without anger, judgment, or mercy. Its “mathematical precision” turns moral responsibility into procedure.

The ending returns to a concise, retrospective narrative mode. The machine and its “idea” perish together, while the chastened inventor becomes gentle, melancholy, and popular with his pupils. This conclusion has the compact symmetry of a moral fable, but its lesson is delivered through irony rather than explicit sermonising. Overall, the style is theatrical, technically detailed, rhetorically inflated, and darkly comic. Its central method is to let an ideology of rationalised punishment elaborate itself at great length, then destroy its pretensions through an exact, bodily, and farcical reversal.

## The Apparatus of Impartial Correction

The public hall of the Provincial Assembly had not been so full since the agricultural exhibition, when a two-headed calf was shown beside a new Belgian threshing machine and received, according to the local newspaper, considerably more attention than the machine.

By seven o’clock every chair was occupied. Schoolmasters stood along the walls; merchants’ wives, rustling in bright dresses, filled the first three rows; officers displayed polished boots and expressions of official endurance. On the right sat representatives of the municipal council, the district court, the prison committee, the temperance society, and the Society for the Encouragement of Useful Knowledge. On the left, beneath a portrait of the Sovereign, sat His Excellency the governor, who was deaf in the left ear and almost deaf in the right. On his knees slept a yellow pug-dog named Hector.

The air was hot and smelled of wax, wool, dust, and perfume. A single fly buzzed against the upper pane with such persistence that several persons looked at it reproachfully.

Upon the stage stood a table, a lectern, a glass of water, and an object of considerable dimensions concealed beneath green baize. From under the cloth protruded two nickel-plated rods, one brass pedal, and something resembling the end of a black leather bench.

At precisely twelve minutes past seven, State Councillor and pedagogue Arkady Arkadyevich Pruzhin mounted the platform.

He was a broad, smooth-faced man of forty-eight, with carefully arranged whiskers, a white waistcoat, and the tranquil forehead of one accustomed to improving others. For twenty-three years he had served the cause of popular education: first as a teacher of penmanship, then as inspector of district schools, and finally as author of several works, among which *The Child as a Future Administrative Unit* had received honourable mention from a committee in Tambov.

He bowed to the governor, to the ladies, to the officers, and separately to the portrait.

“Most respected audience,” he began, “ladies and gentlemen, fathers and mothers, representatives of enlightenment, administration, law, industry, domestic virtue, and our beloved fatherland!”

Hector opened one eye and sneezed.

Arkady Arkadyevich paused until the audience had understood that this was accidental.

“The question which brings us together tonight is ancient, painful, and, I venture to say, unavoidable. How shall we discipline the young? How shall we reform the fallen? How shall we awaken the idle, restrain the violent, admonish the careless, and direct the morally wavering citizen toward the straight and radiant highway of duty?”

The governor cupped a hand to his ear.

“What’s he saying?” he asked his adjutant.

“Discipline, Your Excellency.”

“Quite right. Twenty-five strokes.”

Hector barked once.

A schoolmistress in the third row frowned, but Arkady Arkadyevich, who had heard the recommendation, inclined his head as though acknowledging support from the highest administrative quarter.

“For centuries,” he continued, “these great tasks have been entrusted to the human hand. The father raises his hand against the son; the schoolmaster against the pupil; the sergeant against the recruit; the overseer against the negligent workman. And what follows? Anger! Partiality! Excess! Insufficiency! One child receives three strokes because he has broken a window; another receives seven because the educator’s soup was cold. One soldier is punished weakly because the sergeant likes his singing; another severely because the sergeant has lost at cards. Can this be called justice?”

“No!” cried someone near the door.

“Precisely. It cannot. Conventional corporal punishment, ladies and gentlemen, is barbarous, unscientific, unhygienic, emotionally compromised, administratively inconvenient, and statistically useless.”

There was applause, especially from the schoolmistresses. One young barrister whispered that the speaker was evidently a progressive.

Arkady Arkadyevich drank water.

“And yet,” he said, raising one finger, “must we, because the hand is imperfect, reject the principle embodied by the hand?”

The applause ceased.

“Shall we uproot from Russian soil an institution sanctified by household custom, military experience, monastic practice, proverbial wisdom, and the recollections of our own childhood? No, ladies and gentlemen! A thousand times no! The birch rod, properly understood, is not an instrument of cruelty. It is a national pedagogical symbol. It is, if I may so express myself, the severe but loving comma which Providence places in the unfinished sentence of human misconduct.”

The young barrister stopped smiling.

“We must not abolish correction. We must purify it. We must take it from the trembling, irritable, subjective hand and place it in the calm embrace of mechanism. Steam has transformed transport. Electricity has transformed communication. The calculating machine has transformed accounts. Why, then, should exact science hesitate before the final fortress of disorder—the human posterior?”

A merchant coughed violently into his beard. Several ladies lowered their eyes. The governor, having caught only the last word, nodded.

“Fifty,” he said.

Hector barked twice.

Arkady Arkadyevich turned toward the covered object.

“For eleven years, at the sacrifice of rest, fortune, family tranquillity, and two fingernails, I have laboured upon the solution. Tonight I have the honour to present the first Russian Automatic Apparatus for Impartial Correction, Model P-3, with combined moral, statistical, restraining, and revisionary functions.”

He seized the baize and drew it away.

It is difficult to describe the impression produced upon the public.

The machine resembled at once a dentist’s chair, a railway buffer, a sewing apparatus, and an instrument discovered in the cellar of a medieval castle. Its principal body consisted of an iron frame painted a cheerful blue. In the middle was a sloping leather platform furnished with straps for the wrists, ankles, waist, shoulders, and, for reasons not immediately apparent, the chin. Above the platform rose a steel arm terminating in a bundle of interchangeable rods. On one side were three dials marked **AGE**, **CONSTITUTION**, and **DEGREE OF MORAL OBDURACY**. On the other stood a glass-covered counter. Brass pipes descended into a locked box. A nickel receptacle, shaped like a church collection plate, projected from the front.

The audience was silent. The fly continued its work at the window.

Arkady Arkadyevich laid one hand affectionately upon the frame.

“Do not be alarmed by its appearance. Power without elegance is Asiatic; elegance without power is French. Here, I trust, we have achieved a Russian harmony of both.”

He indicated the dials.

“The operation is simplicity itself. The offender is placed here, face downward, though for certain administrative purposes an alternative position may be selected. The restraining bands close automatically. The operator then sets age, physical condition, and moral category: first degree, inattention; second degree, disobedience; third degree, falsehood; fourth degree, theft; fifth degree, repeated theft with insolence; sixth degree, nihilistic tendency, mockery of superiors, or refusal to confess.”

“And lateness?” called a factory owner.

“Second degree for the first offence, third for repetition, fourth if accompanied by excuses.”

“Excellent!”

“The motive force is obtained from a tempered spring. No steam boiler is required. There is no smoke, no coal, no licensed engineer. One winding provides eight thousand corrective movements, though I recommend inspection after every six thousand, especially in damp weather.”

He removed a birch bundle from the steel arm and replaced it with a narrow leather strap.

“For schools, the birch attachment. For prisons and military establishments, leather. For factories, according to the collective agreement, either may be used. A velvet-covered attachment is under consideration for institutes attended by young ladies of noble birth.”

The schoolmistresses conferred in undertones.

“But who,” asked the young barrister, “decides the number?”

Arkady Arkadyevich smiled. It was the smile of a man who has waited eleven years for that question.

“Nobody.”

He allowed the word to travel through the hall.

“Therein lies the moral grandeur of the invention. Men decide badly. Mechanism decides exactly. Observe the receptacle. Into it is placed a specially issued correction coupon. Each coupon possesses a calibrated weight. One gram represents one stroke. Five grams, five strokes; ten, ten; twenty-five, twenty-five. The coupon bears the offender’s name, offence, date, institution, and signature of the responsible authority. As it falls, a balance descends, the weight is registered, the straps close, the apparatus begins, and the counter records the execution of justice.”

He produced several round brass discs.

“For small institutions, where printed coupons would burden the budget, ordinary coin may be employed. A one-kopeck piece, three strokes; two kopecks, seven; five kopecks, twenty; silver denominations according to a scale provided in Appendix B. Any round object of sufficient weight activates the mechanism.”

“Could a button do it?” asked a boy from the gallery.

“If metal, yes. If bone, probably not, though experiments continue.”

The boy looked respectfully at his coat.

“To prevent sentimental interference,” Arkady Arkadyevich went on, “the apparatus cannot be stopped during operation. This is essential. How often does weakness enter at the seventh stroke and ruin the benefit intended by ten! How often do tears, promises, maternal shrieks, influential relatives, or sudden appeals to Christian mercy interrupt an educational process at its most fruitful stage! Here such abuses are impossible. Once begun, correction proceeds to its mathematically appointed conclusion.”

A thin priest raised his eyebrows.

“In emergencies?” he asked.

“There can be no emergency in exactitude, Father.”

“But if the apparatus malfunctions?”

“It cannot.”

“But if—”

“For the satisfaction of persons whose imagination outruns their reason, two special interruption keys have nevertheless been provided. They must be inserted simultaneously into locks situated on opposite sides. The keys are dissimilar, numbered, and entrusted to separate responsible persons. Thus neither caprice nor panic can obstruct the law.”

He called his attendant, a red-haired former soldier named Spiridon, who came forward carrying two enormous keys on blue ribbons.

“Key A remains with the institution’s director. Key B with the physician, chaplain, senior clerk, or other individual enjoying confidence. Spiridon, show them.”

Spiridon held up the keys.

“Don’t lose them,” said Arkady Arkadyevich.

“Never, Arkady Arkadyevich. I keep them as I keep my own soul.”

“Your soul is not an approved storage location.”

The audience laughed. Spiridon laughed also, after looking around to determine whether he might.

A leather dummy was brought from behind the curtain. It wore a schoolboy’s jacket on its upper half and military trousers on its lower, thereby representing the widest practical range of the invention.

“Let us suppose,” said the lecturer, “that this citizen has broken a window, smoked behind the chapel, stolen six pears, contradicted his mother, failed to salute an officer, and written an anonymous letter to the newspaper. A complex case. Twenty strokes.”

He placed a twenty-gram coupon into the receptacle.

There came a metallic click.

The platform opened like a jaw. Two padded arms seized the dummy and drew it flat. The straps snapped shut. A warning bell sounded with surprising delicacy.

Then:

Whack!

Several ladies started.

Whack! Whack! Whack!

The steel arm rose and fell with sober celerity. The counter displayed 1, 2, 3, 4. At ten strokes a small brass hand moved from a white section marked **RESISTANCE** into a pale blue section marked **REFLECTION**. At eighteen it entered **REPENTANCE**. At twenty the machine stopped, released the straps, rang twice, and stamped a paper certificate.

Spiridon carried the certificate to the governor.

“What’s this?” asked His Excellency.

“Successful correction.”

“Not enough. Give him a hundred.”

Hector, disturbed by the demonstration, barked furiously at the dummy.

The applause lasted nearly a minute.

Arkady Arkadyevich’s cheeks glowed. He walked from dial to dial, explaining the self-cleaning bearings, the winter lubrication, the adjustable velocity, the sanitary leather, the duplicate record cylinder, and the optional drawer in which confiscated sweets, cards, tobacco, political pamphlets, and slingshots might be stored.

He then advanced to the broader consequences.

“Imagine, ladies and gentlemen, not one apparatus, but ten thousand! In every school, punctuality. In every office, diligence. In every regiment, obedience. In every factory, productivity. In every prison, remorse. In every home, peace!”

A mother in the second row whispered that the thing would never fit beside the samovar.

“Consider the economy. At present, punishment consumes the valuable time of teachers, warders, non-commissioned officers, foremen, fathers, guardians, and elder brothers. It causes fatigue of the arm, derangement of the nerves, quarrels, complaints, inquiries, medical certificates, and occasionally lawsuits. The Automatic Corrector eliminates all these.”

“Except medical certificates,” murmured the doctor.

“Crime will disappear because punishment will be certain. Idleness will disappear because correction will be immediate. Budget deficits will disappear because the apparatus, when not occupied with offenders, may stamp envelopes, crack nuts, and, with a special attachment, beat carpets. Even family discord will diminish. The husband need no longer punish in anger; the wife need no longer reproach in tears. Both will refer the matter to the domestic tariff.”

This proposal produced mixed expressions among the married portion of the hall.

“A husband coming home after midnight—fifteen grams. A wife exceeding the household allowance—ten. A child lying—five. A cook spoiling the roast—three, unless intentional. Thus emotion gives way to procedure, procedure to order, and order to prosperity.”

The governor leaned toward his adjutant.

“Is he proposing to flog cooks?”

“Among others, Your Excellency.”

“Two hundred. Cooks are incorrigible.”

Hector yawned.

“And our fatherland,” Arkady Arkadyevich cried, now reaching the loftiest portion of his address, “will stand before Europe not as a backward pupil ashamed of its ancestral rod, but as a mature teacher who has fitted that rod with bearings, indicators, safety valves, and a numbered government seal!”

Applause broke out in several parts of the hall. The factory owner shouted “Bravo!” A police captain demanded information about wholesale prices. The headmaster of the classical gymnasium calculated aloud that two machines would suffice if the lower forms were processed before luncheon.

Arkady Arkadyevich bowed. His triumph was complete.

“One final detail,” he said. “Certain critics have objected that coupons may be falsified. To them I answer with this.”

From his waistcoat pocket he drew a large gold chronometer, presented to him by grateful colleagues on the twentieth anniversary of his service. It was a heavy, splendid object, bearing on its lid a double-headed eagle surrounded by laurel leaves and the inscription: **TO THE UNTIRING SOWER OF REASON**.

“The sensitivity of the balance may be verified by any certified weight. This chronometer, for example, weighs exactly two hundred and twelve grams. Were it round enough to enter the receptacle—and it is—its descent would command, under the present ratio, two thousand one hundred and twenty strokes.”

He held it over the nickel plate.

The hall leaned forward.

“Observe, however, that activation requires actual release. So long as the object remains in my rational control—”

At that instant Hector barked.

Arkady Arkadyevich turned his head. The chronometer slipped between his fingers.

It struck the rim, spun once with a golden flash, and dropped into the receptacle.

Click.

For perhaps half a second nobody understood what had happened.

Then the apparatus opened.

Arkady Arkadyevich attempted to step back, but the lower gripping arm caught him behind the knees. He sat abruptly, waved both hands, and vanished forward onto the leather platform. The wrist straps snapped shut. The ankle clamps closed over his boots. A broad belt fastened itself around his waist, crushing his white waistcoat. Finally the chin strap descended and pressed his face sideways against the cushion.

The warning bell rang.

“No,” said Arkady Arkadyevich.

Whack!

His whole body jumped.

Whack!

“Stop!”

Whack!

The counter showed 3.

Spiridon rushed toward the machine.

“The keys!” cried the lecturer. “Keys, idiot!”

“Immediately, Arkady Arkadyevich!”

Whack! Whack! Whack!

The polished public orator disappeared with astonishing speed. In his place lay a red-faced man kicking inside new trousers and using words not listed in any pedagogical manual.

“Turn it off! Break it! Murderers! Donkeys!”

“Do not excite yourself,” said the doctor, coming onto the stage.

“Whack!”

“You lie there and say that!”

The counter reached 17.

Spiridon searched his coat, his trousers, and his boots. He looked under the table, inside the lectern, beneath the dummy, and finally in his cap.

“Where are the keys?” shouted the police captain.

“I had them in my hands!”

“That is not where they are now!”

“Perhaps I put them down.”

“Where?”

“If I knew where, they wouldn’t be lost.”

Whack! Whack! Whack!

“Twenty-five,” announced the governor, watching the counter. “That ought to be sufficient.”

“It’s already thirty-two, Your Excellency.”

“Then stop.”

“It cannot be stopped.”

“Fifty more for insubordination.”

Hector barked encouragement.

The audience rose. Ladies climbed onto chairs; officers climbed onto the stage. Someone shouted for water. Someone else shouted that water must never be poured on machinery. The headmaster demanded everyone remain calm and was knocked against the dummy by the factory owner.

“Key A!” screamed Arkady Arkadyevich. “Blue ribbon! Key B! Other blue ribbon! Find them!”

“They were both blue?” asked the police captain.

“For aesthetic uniformity—ah!—curse aesthetics!”

The counter showed 74, 75, 76.

The doctor pulled at the waist strap. It tightened automatically.

“Self-adjusting,” groaned the inventor. “I made it self-adjusting.”

The young barrister tried to lift the steel arm. It struck his hat into the audience.

Spiridon crawled under the machine and seized a rod.

“Don’t touch the compensator!” cried Arkady Arkadyevich.

“What’s the compensator?”

“The thing you’re touching!”

A spring released with a bang, and the rate increased.

Whack-whack! Whack-whack! Whack-whack!

The counter passed 100.

It should be said to Spiridon’s credit that his devotion never weakened. His judgment, however, remained unequal to his devotion.

“Cut off the trousers!” ordered the doctor.

“Not the trousers!” Spiridon protested. “They’re new. Thirty-two roubles, from Moscow.”

“Cut them!”

“Cut the straps first!”

“The straps are steel-lined.”

“Then cut around them carefully.”

Arkady Arkadyevich raised his head as far as the chin restraint allowed.

“Spiridon,” he said in a dreadful voice, “if I survive, I will personally put you through this machine with the church bell.”

Whack!

The governor’s adjutant drew his sword and struck the main spring housing. The blade broke. Its upper half flew across the stage, knocked a plaster laurel from the portrait frame, and landed in the lap of the chairwoman of the temperance society.

The machine continued.

237, 238, 239.

The police captain ordered the exits closed, though no one had attempted escape. The factory owner offered five hundred roubles to anyone who stopped the mechanism. Three engineering students began turning different screws. One screw released black oil over the governor’s uniform. Another opened the drawer of confiscated objects, scattering tobacco, nuts, and sample slingshots across the floor. The third caused the certificate printer to issue a paper every ten strokes:

**CORRECTION IN PROGRESS.**

**CORRECTION IN PROGRESS.**

**CORRECTION IN PROGRESS.**

At 318 the priest attempted to comfort the victim.

“Endure, Arkady Arkadyevich. Suffering purifies.”

“It is easy to purify others!” came the reply.

At 401 the electric lamps flickered, though the machine was not connected to them.

At 460 Spiridon found Key A in the pocket of the schoolboy dummy.

“Here!”

“Where is B?”

Silence followed.

The former soldier turned pale.

“I may have placed it somewhere safe.”

“Where is safe?”

“My overcoat.”

“Where is your overcoat?”

“At the railway station.”

The machine maintained mathematical precision.

Whack. 501.

Whack. 502.

Whack. 503.

The first enthusiasm of the public had by now disappeared. The schoolmistresses looked ill. The factory owner no longer asked about wholesale prices. Several mothers silently removed metal buttons from their children’s coats. The headmaster of the gymnasium, who had intended to request two machines, slipped his prospectus beneath a chair.

At 600, the municipal engineer arrived. He walked around the apparatus, tapped it with a pencil, and declared that it had been incorrectly installed.

“It isn’t installed!” cried the barrister. “It’s portable!”

“That explains the instability.”

“Can you stop it?”

“Not without plans.”

“The plans are in my desk,” gasped Arkady Arkadyevich.

“Where is the desk?”

“In my house.”

“Then we require a written requisition for access.”

The police captain threatened to requisition the engineer personally. This accelerated matters but did not improve them.

At 713 the doctor announced that the victim possessed an unusually strong constitution.

“Set the dial to weak!” pleaded Arkady Arkadyevich.

The doctor turned the **CONSTITUTION** indicator. It resisted, then sprang from **ROBUST** to **ATHLETIC**.

The blows became heavier.

The doctor stepped away.

At 800, the audience began counting involuntarily. At first only a clerk near the wall murmured the numbers, but soon others joined him, perhaps because numerical participation gave them the illusion of assistance.

“Eight hundred and eleven… eight hundred and twelve… eight hundred and thirteen…”

“Stop counting!” shrieked Arkady Arkadyevich.

They stopped for six strokes, then resumed in whispers.

The governor had at last understood the seriousness of the situation.

“Use artillery,” he ordered.

“The hall would be damaged, Your Excellency.”

“What sort of provincial hall cannot withstand one shell?”

The adjutant proposed the fire brigade as a compromise.

A messenger was sent.

At 936, Key B was discovered. It hung from Spiridon’s neck beneath his shirt, where he had placed it for absolute security. He wept with joy. Key A was inserted into the left lock, Key B into the right.

“Turn!” commanded the police captain.

They turned.

Nothing happened.

“Opposite directions!” cried Arkady Arkadyevich.

They turned opposite directions.

A small panel opened and displayed the words:

**INTERRUPTION REQUIRES AUTHORISATION SEAL.**

“Where is the seal?”

Arkady Arkadyevich closed his eyes.

“In my desk.”

The engineer nodded. “As I anticipated.”

At 1,000 strokes, the machine rang ceremonially, stamped a larger certificate, and shifted the indicator from **REPENTANCE** to **MORAL RENEWAL**.

Arkady Arkadyevich no longer insulted anyone. He asked only, in a quiet and astonished voice, whether it was still going.

It was.

The fire brigade arrived at 1,127 with helmets, axes, hooks, two hoses, and a red wagon drawn by exhausted horses. Its chief, a small man with a magnificent black beard, surveyed the scene.

“Fire?”

“No.”

“Smoke?”

“No.”

“Then why were we called?”

“To destroy a pedagogical instrument.”

The chief considered this unusual but not beyond municipal experience.

The firemen first attempted water. A jet struck the apparatus, ricocheted from its casing, drenched the first six rows, and knocked the governor backward over his chair. Hector escaped into the orchestra enclosure and barked there with increased authority.

The machine, washed and shining, continued.

1,204. 1,205. 1,206.

Axes were brought down upon the outer housing. Blue enamel flew. One fireman lost his helmet; another struck the counter, which spun to 9,999, returned to 1,231, and proceeded accurately from there.

“Careful with the counter!” cried the municipal clerk. “It is required for the report.”

The chief ordered crowbars. The iron frame bent but held. The floorboards cracked. The platform tilted, carrying Arkady Arkadyevich with it, while the corrective arm adjusted its angle and continued its duty.

1,390.

1,391.

1,392.

The lecturer’s commemorative chronometer could be heard rattling inside the balance chamber at each stroke, untiringly sowing reason.

At 1,500, the chief lost patience.

“Break everything,” he said.

Six firemen attacked at once. They smashed the spring box, tore away the certificate printer, severed two rods, split the blue casing, and drove a hook through the principal gear. The apparatus hesitated.

Whack.

1,647.

A gear screamed.

Whack.

1,648.

The steel arm rose slowly, as though reconsidering its entire philosophy.

Whack.

1,649.

Everyone held his breath.

The arm descended one last time.

Whack.

1,650.

Then the machine gave a deep metallic sigh. Springs burst from its side. The counter fell off. The restraining straps opened, the leather platform collapsed, and Arkady Arkadyevich slid gently onto the wet floor among brass coupons, broken rods, official certificates, and fragments of the inscription **IMPARTIAL CORRECTION**.

Thus perished the apparatus, having completed one thousand six hundred and fifty strokes out of the two thousand one hundred and twenty assigned to it by mechanical justice.

The idea perished somewhat sooner.

Arkady Arkadyevich remained in bed for three months. The provincial newspaper reported that his indisposition had resulted from “an unforeseen technical misunderstanding during a highly successful scientific demonstration.” The governor recommended him for a medal, then forgot the matter. Spiridon returned the trousers to the Moscow tailor, who declined all responsibility.

In autumn Arkady Arkadyevich resumed teaching.

Those who had known him before observed a remarkable change. He no longer spoke of the child as an administrative unit. He ceased writing regulations. When a pupil came late, he asked whether the road was muddy. When a boy broke a window, he first examined the putty. He forgave noise, clumsiness, ink stains, forgotten books, and even whispering during geography. His voice became low; his step cautious; his expression gentle and permanently melancholy.

The pupils loved him.

Sometimes, during arithmetic, when a child recited numbers in a steady sequence—forty-seven, forty-eight, forty-nine—Arkady Arkadyevich would grow pale and ask him to begin again from another place.

He never rebuilt the apparatus, never mentioned mechanical justice, and would not carry coins.

As for the golden chronometer, it was recovered from the wreckage, flattened almost beyond recognition. Arkady Arkadyevich kept it in a drawer without having it repaired. Beneath the crushed double-headed eagle, the final words of the inscription could still be read:

**THE UNTIRING SOWER OF REASON.**

# The Museum of Unfinished Things

Every morning at nine, Mara Vale unlocked the front doors of the Museum of Unfinished Things and waited for someone to visit.

Usually, no one did.

The museum stood at the quiet end of Bellweather Street, between a boarded-up bakery and a narrow shop that repaired clocks. Its stone facade was grander than the building deserved. Four marble pillars held up a cracked pediment, and above the bronze doors, faded gold letters announced:

**THE MUSEUM OF UNFINISHED THINGS**

Inside, beneath glass and dust, rested the abandoned efforts of generations.

There was a symphony without its final movement, donated by the grandchildren of a composer who had died convinced that the missing notes would come to him in a dream. There was a bridge in miniature, built from iron and hope, which had never crossed a river. There were novels ending halfway through a sentence, wedding dresses missing sleeves, inventions lacking essential gears, and one wooden staircase that climbed thirteen steps before stopping in midair.

Mara’s job was to care for them all.

She polished the glass cases. She adjusted the labels. She repaired whatever could be repaired without making anything complete.

That last rule was the museum’s oldest and strictest.

**An unfinished thing must remain unfinished.**

The museum’s founder had written it in black ink across the first page of the staff handbook. No explanation followed.

Mara had worked there for eleven years. She knew every incomplete object as another person might know neighbors. She knew that the headless marble horse in Gallery Two gathered dust fastest around its broken neck. She knew that the half-painted portrait of a laughing woman seemed sadder in winter. She knew that if the west windows were opened during rain, the pages of the unfinished encyclopedia turned by themselves until they reached the unwritten entry for “Home.”

She also knew that the museum was dying.

On a Monday in October, the director called her into his office.

Mr. Rook was a thin man with a silver mustache and the permanent expression of someone listening to bad news through a wall.

“We received a letter from the council,” he said.

Mara sat opposite him. On the desk between them lay an envelope stamped with the city seal.

“They’re withdrawing our funding,” he continued. “At the end of the month.”

Mara stared at him. “Then we’ll charge admission.”

“We tried that in 1987. Attendance fell.”

“We could host lectures.”

“About incompletion?”

“About history. Art. Failure.”

“People prefer success.”

Mara looked through the office window toward the central hall. In its middle stood the museum’s largest exhibit: an unfinished ship built by an unknown carpenter. Its ribs curved upward like the bones of a whale. No mast had ever been fitted. No sails had ever been sewn. Yet Mara had always thought it looked ready to depart.

“What happens to the collection?” she asked.

“Some objects will go into storage. Some will be returned to their donors. Others will be sold.”

“Sold to whom?”

“Anyone who wants them.”

The answer struck her as obscene. She imagined the laughing woman’s portrait hanging above a restaurant table, its blank corner stained with grease. She imagined the symphony’s pages cut apart and framed. She imagined the staircase used as firewood.

“There must be something we can do.”

Mr. Rook removed his spectacles and cleaned them with a handkerchief. “The council has offered us one possibility. If we can attract five thousand visitors before the last day of the month, they’ll reconsider.”

Mara nearly laughed. The museum had welcomed three hundred and twelve visitors during the previous year. Seventy had been schoolchildren who believed they were going to the natural history museum across town.

“Five thousand?”

“Yes.”

“In three weeks?”

“Yes.”

Mr. Rook replaced his spectacles. “I have already begun preparing an inventory for closure.”

Mara stood.

“Don’t,” she said.

“Mara—”

“Not yet.”

She left his office and walked through the galleries.

At ten, an elderly tourist entered, asked whether the museum had a restroom, and departed without viewing the collection.

At noon, rain began tapping the windows.

At three, Mara sat beneath the unfinished ship and listened to the old building creak.

Five thousand visitors.

She considered advertising. The museum had no budget. She considered writing to newspapers, but newspapers wanted scandals, murders, miracles, and royal weddings. An assortment of abandoned projects would interest no one.

Unless one of them were no longer abandoned.

Her eyes moved toward the eastern gallery, where a locked door stood behind a velvet rope.

The door led to the Archive of Dangerous Fragments.

Mara had entered the archive only twice, both times with Mr. Rook. It contained unfinished things judged too unstable for public exhibition: a map of places that did not exist, a mechanical bird that whispered the names of people who would vanish, and a silver mirror that reflected its subjects as they might have been.

There was also, Mara remembered, an unfinished story.

According to museum records, it had been discovered in 1846 inside the walls of a demolished house. The author was unknown. The surviving manuscript consisted of forty-seven handwritten pages and ended with a single incomplete line:

**When the last door opened, she saw—**

Several curators had attempted to study it. Each reported vivid dreams. One disappeared for six days and returned with sand in his shoes, though he had never left the city. In 1911, a copyist tried to complete the final sentence. The words vanished from the page, along with the copyist’s ability to read.

The manuscript had been locked away ever since.

Mara knew the rule.

An unfinished thing must remain unfinished.

She also knew rules were often the polished surfaces of old fears. People remembered the warning and forgot the reason.

At half past five, after Mr. Rook had gone home, Mara took the archive key from his office.

The eastern gallery smelled of stone and varnish. She unhooked the velvet rope, unlocked the door, and descended a narrow staircase.

The archive lay underground. Shelves disappeared into darkness, burdened with boxes, cabinets, and shrouded shapes. Mara switched on a green-shaded lamp and located the manuscript in a locked drawer.

It was wrapped in blue cloth.

She carried it upstairs to the curator’s desk and untied the ribbon.

The pages were yellow but perfectly preserved. The handwriting leaned sharply forward, as if every sentence were running out of time.

Mara began to read.

The story concerned a young woman named Elianor who lived in a city where every door opened to the same room. Her mother had disappeared behind one of those doors, and Elianor believed that somewhere there must be an entrance leading elsewhere. She searched cellars, palaces, prisons, and towers. Each door brought her back to the room: four gray walls, one wooden chair, and another closed door.

The story was strange, repetitive, and impossible to put down.

As Mara read, the museum became very quiet. Rain trembled against the roof. The electric lights dimmed.

Elianor crossed the city. She grew older. Friends abandoned her. Authorities arrested her. Still she searched. At last she found a door beneath the roots of a dead tree outside the city walls.

Mara reached the final page.

**Elianor placed her hand upon the golden handle. All her life had led to this threshold. Behind her stood the city of one room; before her waited everything she had been denied. She turned the handle. The last door opened.**

Then came the unfinished line.

**When the last door opened, she saw—**

Mara held her breath.

The empty space below the words seemed enormous. It pulled at her imagination like a well.

What had Elianor seen?

Her mother? Another world? Herself?

Mara picked up a pencil.

She told herself she only wanted to test the old story about the copyist. She would add one word in the margin, observe the result, and erase it.

The pencil hovered over the paper.

At that moment, somewhere in the museum, a door slammed.

Mara jumped. The pencil struck the final page, leaving a tiny gray mark.

From the central hall came the groan of bending timber.

She hurried out.

The unfinished ship was moving.

Its wooden ribs rose and fell as though breathing. Planks slid from the exhibition platform and fastened themselves along the hull. Nails rolled across the floor, then leaped into place. A mast pushed upward toward the glass ceiling.

Mara watched, horrified, as years of missing work completed itself in seconds.

The ship became whole.

Then it vanished.

It did not fade or dissolve. One moment it stood in the hall; the next, there was only an empty platform and the scent of salt water.

Behind Mara, music began to play.

The unfinished symphony’s pages fluttered inside their case. Invisible instruments filled the museum with a final movement no living orchestra had performed. The melody climbed, beautiful and terrible, toward its conclusion.

When the last note sounded, the pages vanished.

“No,” Mara whispered.

A cracking noise came from Gallery Two.

The headless marble horse had grown a head. It shook dust from its mane, shattered the glass around it, and galloped through the wall without leaving a hole.

All around the museum, unfinished things completed themselves and disappeared.

The laughing woman acquired a painted hand and a blue background, smiled directly at Mara, and stepped backward out of the canvas.

The miniature bridge extended beyond its display table, shrinking into an impossible distance.

The staircase in the western hall grew a fourteenth step, then a fifteenth, rising through the ceiling toward stars visible beyond the roof.

Mara ran back to the manuscript.

The pencil mark had changed. It was no longer a simple line. Letters formed slowly across the paper in Mara’s own handwriting.

**When the last door opened, she saw a way out.**

Beneath that sentence appeared another.

**And everything unfinished followed her.**

Mara seized an eraser and rubbed at the words. The paper tore, but the writing remained.

Upstairs, glass shattered. Wind roared through the galleries. Pages flew like birds.

Mara grabbed the manuscript and raced toward Mr. Rook’s office, where the original handbook was kept in a fireproof cabinet.

She found it beneath a stack of tax records. The leather binding had cracked, and the founder’s warning remained on the first page.

**An unfinished thing must remain unfinished.**

This time Mara turned the page.

There was more.

The ink had faded almost to brown.

**Completion is not perfection. It is departure. Every unfinished work remains among us because it still belongs partly to this world. Finish it, and it must go where finished things go.**

On the next page, the founder had written:

**If the Last Story is ever completed, the boundary will open. Every fragment will seek its ending, and our world, which is itself unfinished, may follow.**

Mara looked toward the office window.

Outside, the city was changing.

Across the street, the clockmaker’s sign gained a final painted letter. The shop vanished. At the end of Bellweather Street, construction workers fled from a half-built apartment block as windows appeared across its bare concrete walls. Once complete, the whole building flickered and disappeared.

It was spreading.

Every unfinished song, every abandoned letter, every half-knitted scarf and interrupted apology would complete itself. And then—

Our world, which is itself unfinished, may follow.

Mara returned to the manuscript. She tried crossing out the final sentence. She tried tearing away the bottom of the page. Each strip of paper vanished from her fingers and reappeared whole.

The story had an ending now. It could not be made incomplete by ordinary damage.

But perhaps it could be continued.

Mara pulled a blank sheet from the printer and placed it after the final page. With shaking hands, she wrote:

**But Elianor did not step through.**

Nothing happened.

The sentence sat on the new paper, separate and powerless.

Mara realized the manuscript would not accept an ending merely placed beside it. The story had chosen its own words from her accidental mark. To change it, she would have to enter it where it lived.

The silver mirror.

She ran to the archive.

Objects were disappearing from shelves. A clock missing its minute hand suddenly chimed, became whole, and winked out. An incomplete suit of armor filled itself with a knight who saluted Mara before dissolving into sparks.

At the back of the archive stood the mirror, covered by a black cloth.

Mara tore the cloth away.

The silver surface did not show her reflection.

It showed Mara as she might have been.

In the mirror, she stood on a brightly lit stage while an audience applauded. Her hair was shorter, her face younger. She wore a black evening dress and held a violin.

Mara stepped back.

She had studied music once. She had dreamed of performing. But at twenty-three, terrified of failing an audition, she had put her violin under her bed. A temporary decision, she had told herself.

The museum had hired her a month later.

In the mirror, the other Mara bowed.

Then the image changed.

She saw herself older, sitting beside a hospital bed, holding her father’s hand. In reality, she had arrived too late.

The image changed again.

A sunlit kitchen. A child laughing. A garden. A red front door. A life completed from choices she had never made.

The mirror offered not truth, but possibility. Unfinished lives, waiting beyond the glass.

Mara placed the manuscript against its surface.

The mirror rippled.

The pages passed through.

She followed.

For an instant, she fell through every life she had not lived.

She was a musician. A mother. A traveler. A woman who had married. A woman who had refused. A woman who had left the city at nineteen and never returned. A woman who had died young. A woman who had become cruel. A woman who had been brave at exactly the right moment.

Then she landed on hard ground beneath a white sky.

Before her stood a golden door.

A young woman held its handle.

“Elianor!” Mara shouted.

The woman turned. She was old and young at once, her face shifting with every year of her long search.

Behind her, through the open door, lay a vast blue sea. The completed ship sailed toward the horizon. The marble horse galloped along the shore. Music moved through the air in visible ribbons.

Thousands of finished things crossed into that shining world.

“It’s beautiful,” Elianor said.

“Yes,” Mara answered. “But you can’t go.”

Elianor’s expression hardened. “I have spent my life looking for this.”

“I know.”

“My mother is there.”

Beyond the doorway stood a woman in a green coat, holding out her arms.

Mara felt the ache of it. Every absence mended. Every regret answered. Every effort rewarded with an ending.

“What right do you have to stop me?” Elianor demanded.

“None.”

“Then let me pass.”

“If you do, my world may disappear.”

“Your world?” Elianor laughed bitterly. “Your world left me searching for forty-seven pages and abandoned me at the threshold.”

Mara looked back.

Behind them stretched the city of one room. Every open doorway revealed the same gray walls and wooden chair. It was a prison made by an author who had never decided what lay beyond it.

“You deserved an ending,” Mara said.

“Yes.”

“But not one chosen by accident.”

Elianor glanced through the golden doorway.

Her mother waited beside the sea.

“What else can I do?”

Mara remembered the blank sheet she had tried to add. A story could not be undone once finished. But an ending did not have to be a wall. Sometimes it could be a door into something larger.

“Choose for yourself,” Mara said.

“That is what I’m doing.”

“No. You’re choosing between the room and the answer someone else gave you. There may be more choices.”

Elianor looked at the city behind her. “There are no other doors.”

“Then make one.”

For a long moment, neither moved.

The white sky began to crack. Through the fractures Mara glimpsed the museum, the city, and darkness gathering at the edges of both.

Elianor released the golden handle.

She walked to the nearest gray wall.

From her coat, she drew a piece of chalk.

“Will this work?” she asked.

“I don’t know.”

“That is not a satisfying answer.”

“It’s the only honest one.”

Elianor smiled.

On the wall, she drew the outline of a door.

The golden doorway trembled. The sea beyond it folded like painted cloth. The waiting mother raised one hand—not in farewell, Mara thought, but in blessing.

Elianor finished the chalk door except for a small gap at the bottom.

Everything stopped.

The sea, the ship, the horse, and the ribbons of music froze. The cracks in the sky ceased spreading.

Elianor placed her fingers against the chalk handle.

“Don’t complete it,” Mara warned.

“I won’t.”

She pushed.

The incomplete door opened.

Beyond it lay neither paradise nor the gray room, but a forest at dawn. A path wound between black trees, disappearing into mist. The destination was impossible to see.

Elianor laughed.

This time, her face did not shift. She looked young, though not as young as when her journey began.

“What’s there?” Mara asked.

“I don’t know.”

Elianor stepped into the forest.

The story closed around her.

Mara woke on the archive floor.

The silver mirror stood above her, cracked from corner to corner. It reflected only her ordinary face.

In her hands lay the manuscript.

She turned to the final page.

The accidental ending was gone. In its place, the last lines read:

**When the last door opened, she saw a way out. But she had learned enough of doors to distrust the ones that promised destinations. So Elianor drew another, left it unfinished, and went through.**

Below that, in smaller handwriting, was one final sentence.

**Where she went next is another story.**

The museum had become silent.

Mara climbed the stairs.

Most exhibits had returned. The ship stood unfinished in the central hall, its bare ribs casting long shadows. The symphony lacked its final movement. The marble horse was headless once more.

A few things were gone forever.

The painting of the laughing woman remained an empty canvas. The miniature bridge now led to a real valley visible through a hole no larger than a coin. And the wooden staircase had acquired one additional step.

Outside, Bellweather Street had returned.

Dawn was breaking.

Mr. Rook arrived at eight and found Mara sitting beneath the ship with the manuscript on her knees.

He listened to her story without interruption.

When she finished, he looked ten years older.

“You broke the rule,” he said.

“Yes.”

“You nearly erased the world.”

“Yes.”

“And you entered a dangerous fictional reality through an enchanted mirror.”

“Yes.”

Mr. Rook sighed. “The paperwork will be appalling.”

At nine, they opened the museum.

The first visitor arrived at nine fifteen. Then came three more. By noon, a crowd filled Bellweather Street.

Someone had filmed the disappearing apartment block. Others had recorded music coming from the museum and a marble horse galloping across rooftops. The videos had spread across the world during the night.

Reporters gathered beneath the gold-lettered sign. Historians demanded explanations. Musicians begged to see the symphony. Five thousand visitors arrived before sunset.

The council restored the museum’s funding the following week.

Mr. Rook created a new exhibition titled **The Night the World Nearly Ended**, though Mara objected to the word “nearly.”

The unfinished story remained locked in the archive.

Years passed. The museum expanded into the old bakery and the clockmaker’s shop. People came from distant countries to see the things that had been begun but never completed.

Some visitors laughed at the exhibits. Others wept.

Many recognized something of themselves.

Mara eventually became the director. On her first day in the office, she opened the founder’s handbook and added a line beneath the old warning.

The new rule read:

**An unfinished thing must remain unfinished—unless it learns how to continue.**

She still cared for the collection. She still polished cases and adjusted labels. But once a year, after closing time, she took out the violin she had left beneath her bed for decades.

At first, she played badly.

Then she played less badly.

She never became the woman in the mirror, bowing before a brilliant audience. That life was gone, if it had ever existed. Her father remained dead. The sunlit kitchen belonged to no one she knew. Some doors, once missed, could not be reopened.

But in the central hall, beneath the ribs of the ship that had sailed once and might sail again, Mara practiced.

She did not play symphonies.

She played scales, fragments, and melodies without names. She began songs and abandoned them. She returned to them months later, changing the rhythm or adding a few uncertain notes.

And sometimes, when she paused with the bow lifted and the last note still trembling in the air, she heard something beyond the museum walls.

Not applause.

Not an ending.

Only footsteps on a forest path, moving deeper into the unknown.
